Welcome to Accessible HTML5

This is a well-structured, accessible HTML5 document demonstrating modern best practices for semantic markup and inclusive design.

It uses semantic landmarks, a skip link for keyboard navigation, and CSS that adapts to your light or dark mode preference.

Text and link colors meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes, type scales with your browser's font size, and motion respects your system settings.

Features

  • Semantic HTML structure with proper landmarks
  • Keyboard accessible navigation and focus management
  • Dark mode support with custom color schemes
  • Responsive typography using modern CSS
  • Print-friendly styles for better readability
  • WCAG AA contrast compliance in all color modes

Examples

Component Cards

Card components are useful for organizing related content. They include a subtle border and padding for visual separation.

Learn more about accessibility resources

Interactive Elements

Buttons and links are fully accessible with clear focus states. All interactive elements include visible focus indicators and proper ARIA labels.

Keyboard navigation: Use Tab to move forward, Shift+Tab to move backward, and Enter or Space to activate.

Accessible Form

Contact Information
For example, name@example.com

Click the button to announce a message using a live region. This demonstrates how screen readers are notified of dynamic updates.

content.text:
Looking at this well-structured HTML5 document, I can see several practical improvements to make:

1. **Performance**: Add resource hints (dns-prefetch, preconnect) for external links
2. **Navigation**: Add `aria-current="page"` to nav items to indicate current section
3. **Form**: Enhance with more input type examples (tel, text with patterns)
4. **Content**: Add a code examples section to make the page more educational
5. **Accessibility**: Improve live region announcements with more context

Let me implement these improvements:

Code Examples

Semantic HTML Structure

Use semantic elements to give your HTML meaning. Screen readers and assistive technologies rely on proper element usage.

<header>
  <nav aria-label="Main navigation">
    <ul>
      <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
      <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
    </ul>
  </nav>
</header>
<main id="main">
  <article>
    <h1>Article Title</h1>
    <p>Article content...</p>
  </article>
</main>
<footer>
  <p>© 2026 Your Name</p>
</footer>

ARIA Labels and Descriptions

Use ARIA attributes to provide additional context when semantic HTML alone isn't enough.

<!-- Label a button with aria-label -->
<button aria-label="Close dialog">×</button>

<!-- Describe an input with aria-describedby -->
<input type="password" aria-describedby="pwd-hint">
<small id="pwd-hint">8+ characters, with uppercase and numbers</small>

<!-- Use aria-live for dynamic updates -->
<div aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
  <span id="status"></span>
</div>

Focus Management

Ensure focus is always visible and moves logically through the page using keyboard navigation.

/* Always show focus outlines */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #0052a3;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

/* Skip link for keyboard users */
.skip-link:focus {
  transform: translateY(0);
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1000;
}

Resources
